This page holds the statistical detail behind the [organizer summary](en.qmd). Every number is read from the simulation outputs when the site is rendered. The model, its assumptions and the sources are on the [Methods](methods.qmd), [Assumptions](assumptions.qmd) and [Literature](literature.qmd) pages.

Two kinds of interval appear. An interval "of the median" is a 95% bootstrap interval for the typical night. A "range across nights" covers 5% to 95% of the simulated nights and shows how different one plausible night is from another.

## What was observed and what matches it

The 2026 observations come from the attendees who ran this study. At 15:30 buying was relatively quick, although it still took a while. Between 18:00 and 20:00 (God Module and Das Ich) the beer exchange line alone took more than 40 minutes for a person who already held tickets, both the ticket line and the exchange lines were long, and a lot of people gave up. The longest wait was not measured. The calibration test on the exchange line is two-sided: the median wait of the people who joined it between 18:00 and 20:00 is at least 35 min (over 40 observed, 5 min of tolerance) and at most 70 min. The upper limit is an assumption of the study author, without an observation behind it. A night whose median is not reached by the end of the shortened run fails the upper limit. In the scenario runs of the 2026 setup the median was reached in 100% of the nights. After 20:00 they stopped trying to buy, so every wait after that hour is a prediction of the model. The hall was near its fullest around 22:00. One window sold tickets for every drink, two lines exchanged beer and one exchanged cocktails and shots, and people bought several beers per visit for friends.

Waits are reported as the median time until service, estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method. A person who gave up waited at least until leaving the line, and counting that time as a completed wait would understate lines in which many people give up.

The unknown inputs (how many people drink and how fast, patience, group size, people serving beer, time per ticket sale and per beer) were sampled with a sequential approximate Bayesian computation sampler. Of 8\,960 simulated nights in 6 stages, 268 pass every test in the last stage (effective sample size 62). A weighted resample of 64 nights is used for everything below. In those nights 2 to 5 people serve beer, the ticket window takes a median of 31 s per buyer and the first beer of a visit 58 s.

In the matching nights, between 18:00 and 20:00, the ticket line holds 52 people and the beer exchange lines 83. A person who joins an exchange line waits 48 min (range across nights 31 to 78), the ticket window takes 30 min, and a buyer without tickets needs 96 min for the whole purchase (52 to 152). Between 18:00 and 02:00 9 of 10 buyers in the 2026 setup wait at most 119 min (65 to 191). The predicted wait in the exchange line at 21:30 to 22:30 is 96 min (56 to 155). The hall holds 1\,600 people at its fullest (range across nights 1\,322 to 1\,731), and the bar sells 2\,576 beers (1\,487 to 3\,893). The width of that last range is the reason the number of beers sold in 2026 is the first record requested from the organizers.

![](assets/figures/01_calibration_posterior.png){fig-alt="Range tried and matching values for each unknown input"}

The two line tests require at least 20 people in each line. A stricter reading of 30 people keeps about half of the nights. The plan performs as follows in the two groups.

|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| at least 30 in each line | 37 | 130 | 2.8 | +3,362 |
| 20 to 30 in one of the lines | 11 | 67 | 2.0 | +3,741 |

|:--|:--|

## Effect of each setup

Every setup reruns the same 48 nights with the same people and the same random seed, so each difference is that night's counterfactual. The plan is payment at the serving station with 8 stations and 12 roaming sellers on the floor from 18:00 to 02:30. The wait of 1 in 10 buyers is taken over everyone who joins a line between 18:00 and 02:00, the hours in which lines formed in 2026.

|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 4 ticket windows | -8.0 (-12.4 to -4.0) | +10 (+0 to +16) | 43 of 48 (at least 77%) | < 0.001 |
| Tickets sold with entry + 5-packs | -7.0 (-11.0 to -2.4) | +26 (+16 to +42) | 40 of 48 (at least 70%) | < 0.001 |
| 2026 setup + 6 roaming sellers | -45.3 (-51.1 to -37.6) | +1,920 (+1,851 to +2,101) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| 2026 setup + 2-station satellite bar | -35.8 (-50.9 to -30.9) | +1,011 (+961 to +1,156) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |
| Pay at the station (card/cash), same staff | -15.8 (-21.5 to -13.5) | +369 (+307 to +392) | 46 of 48 (at least 86%) | < 0.001 |
| Cashless wristband at the station, same staff | -24.1 (-29.9 to -16.9) | +546 (+489 to +622) | 47 of 48 (at least 89%) | < 0.001 |

| Plan (pay at the station, recommended crew) | -113.1 (-133.6 to -100.9) | +3,393 (+2,973 to +3,738) | 48 of 48 (at least 93%) | < 0.001 |


![](assets/figures/05_counterfactual_effects.png){fig-alt="Effect of each setup on the wait, beers sold and abandoned attempts"}

With the plan the wait of 1 in 10 buyers falls by 113\.1 min (interval of the median 100\.9 to 133\.6) to 2\.7 min, and the bar sells 3\,393 more beers (2\,973 to 3\,738; range across nights 2\,190 to 4\,604). At an assumed MXN 80 per beer that is MXN 271\,440 in sales (237\,840 to 299\,040). Costs of staff and card fees are not in this figure.

![](assets/figures/04_wait_by_time.png){fig-alt="Typical time in line by time of joining for each setup against 2026"}

## The plan against the alternatives

Differences on the same night, second setup minus first, with the 95% interval of the median.

| Comparison | Wait of 1 in 10 buyers | Beers sold | Staff |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Pay at the station with the 2026 head count, then the plan | \-98\.7 min \(\-106\.2 to \-87\.4\) | \+3\,000 \(\+2\,716 to \+3\,322\) | \+16 |
| The plan, then wristbands + satellite bar + 4 sellers | \+26\.8 min \(\+20\.0 to \+34\.4\) | \-443 \(\-681 to \-253\) | \-10 |
| Card or cash at the station, then cashless wristbands | \-6\.3 min \(\-7\.6 to \-4\.9\) | \+192 \(\+172 to \+237\) | \+0 |

Roaming sellers sell 60% of the beers under the plan (range across nights 53% to 68%). A seller carries 6 beers per trip and refills at an end of the bar in 2 min. There were no sellers in 2026, so these rules are assumptions, and the crew without sellers is the fallback.

Payment at the station with the same head count as 2026 leaves a wait of 101\.2 min for 1 in 10 buyers (up to 148\.4 min in the worst 5% of nights).

## Staffing reliability

A night meets the target when 9 of 10 buyers who join a line between 18:00 and 02:00 wait at most 10 min and at most 5% of purchase attempts are abandoned. Each crew runs on 64 nights. Two crews are chosen per ticket level, each the one with the fewest staff hours among the crews that meet the target in a required share of the nights: the minimum crew (90%) and the recommended crew (95%). The plan uses the recommended crew. For 2\,000 tickets the recommended crew (8 stations, 12 sellers) meets the target in 61 of 64 nights (exact 95% interval 87% to 99%), and the minimum crew (6 stations, 12 sellers) in 59 of 64 (83% to 97%).

![](assets/figures/12_staffing_reliability.png){fig-alt="Share of nights in which each crew meets the waiting target, by ticket level"}

The bad night is the 90th percentile across nights.

In 2026 about 4 people handled beer, counting the ticket window (3 to 6 across nights). The plan uses 20 and 165 more staff hours. On the same night, each extra staff hour sells 21 more beers (95% interval of the median 19 to 23; range across nights 13 to 32), or MXN 1\,710 in sales at the assumed price (1\,550 to 1\,800). Staff, card fees and equipment costs are not included.

## Capacity

The free floor (audience area without vendor strips and tables) is 663 m². At 2\,000 tickets the people standing on it at the fullest moment amount to 2\.07 per m². NFPA 101 caps assembly areas of up to 930 m² at 2\.2 people/m², and the free floor reaches that value near 2\,100 tickets. For larger areas the cap is 1\.54 people/m², which the free floor reaches below 1\,500 tickets\, the lowest level simulated. The free floor is below 930 m² and the whole audience area, with vendor strips and tables, is above it. The hall size comes from a satellite image without a scale bar, with an uncertainty near 10% per side. A hall that much smaller or larger reaches the first value at 1\,700 or 2\,600 tickets. That range comes from rescaling the floor area, without new simulations. The licensed capacity is the legal limit.

![](assets/figures/13_capacity.png){fig-alt="People per m² of free floor at the fullest moment against tickets sold"}

## Serving options

In 2026 every beer was opened and poured into a cup, and the calibrated serving time per beer includes that work. Each option below removes an assumed number of seconds per beer or per payment (`config/serving.yaml`; none of them was measured). Each option runs the whole crew grid at 2\,000 tickets on the 64 staffing nights with the staffing seeds, so the options differ only in the serving time (`scripts/run_serving.py`). The saving per beer is capped at three quarters of the serving time. Sellers keep their own sale time in every option.

The plan on the other pages uses the 2026 practice (opening and pouring). The savings come from our judgement of the time it takes to open a bottle and pour it into a cup; timing a few sales at the next edition would replace them.

## Time-series models

A regression of beers sold per 5 minutes on people inside and a changeover indicator, with AR(1) errors, was fitted on each night from 18:00 to 02:00. In 2026 each extra 100 people inside added \-0\.01 beers per 5 minutes and with the plan 3\.70. A bar whose sales do not follow the crowd is at its limit. The event study shows the lines building after each set ends.

![](assets/figures/09_time_series_models.png){fig-alt="Event study of people in lines around the end of a set and AR(1) regression coefficients"}

## Drinking

With faster service the share of attendees who drink 6 beers or more rises from 2\.1% to 19\.0% (range across nights 8\.1% to 30\.3%). Abbott and Abbott (2000) recommend purchase limits and refusing service to intoxicated patrons, and alcohol was the most common arrest reason in the stadium survey of Ammon and Fried (1999).

## Sensitivity to the calibration settings

The current calibration is compared with two earlier runs on the same hall layout. Each comparison gives the median night and, in brackets, the range across nights (5% to 95%). The runs simulate different nights, so outcomes are compared with a Mann-Whitney U test and shares of nights with Fisher's exact test. The crew table lists every minimum and recommended crew of either run with the nights in which it meets the service target under each calibration. The staffing grid of every run was run with the current settings (64 nights per crew, 0 to 12 sellers). The plan rows of an earlier run use the crew that run recommended under the rule of its time (90% of 32 nights, at most 9 sellers).

## Limits of the study

- The calibration rests on the account of the attendees who ran this study. Sales, entries and service times were not measured.
- People walk in straight lines and pass through each other, so the model cannot compare line layouts, barriers or walkways. Those recommendations come from the literature.
- Cocktails and shots, food, restrooms and evacuation are outside the model.
- There were no roaming sellers in 2026, so the seller rules (how far a seller is seen, time per sale, beers per trip, refill time) are assumed. Under the plan the sellers sell 60% of the beer, so the recommended crews depend on those rules.
- The hall size is an estimate from a satellite image.
- Sales in MXN use an assumed price and exclude costs.

## Reproducing the results

The commands below rebuild every output from the configuration files. The steps and their inputs are described on the [Methods](methods.qmd) page.

```bash
uv sync --group site && rv sync && rv activate
./scripts/run_all.sh
```
